engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: Discovered Attack
chess.body: Moving one piece reveals an attack from another. The moved piece itself may also attack something. Discovered checks are devastating — the opponent must deal with the check while you capture elsewhere. Pattern: move a blocking piece with tempo, reveal a rook/bishop attack. Double attacks are impossible to fully defend.

wisdom.title: Simplicity is the Path to Happiness
wisdom.body: Happiness research consistently shows: strong relationships + meaningful work + enough (not excessive) money = high life satisfaction. You're already building all three. Don't confuse complexity for progress. The man who simplifies wins. Less decisions, less noise, less comparison.

book.author: Ray Dalio
book.lesson: Dalio's formula for growth: Pain + Reflection = Progress. Every painful experience — a mistake, a failure, a loss — contains information that, if properly processed, makes you better. The mistake most people make is avoiding pain (denial, blame) or wallowing in it (self-pity, rumination) without converting it into learning. Dalio's habit after any significant setback: write down what happened, what you could have done differently, and what principle you need to update or add. He built Bridgewater's entire operating manual from 40 years of documented mistakes and learnings.
book.key_quote: Your mistakes are your most valuable teachers. Only those who extract the lesson grow faster than those who don't make mistakes at all.
book.action: After your next significant failure or setback, write a post-mortem: what happened, why, what you'd do differently, what principle to add.
crux: Pain + reflection = progress. Pain alone teaches nothing.
Radical truth and radical transparency, applied consistently, beat politeness.
Embrace reality and deal with it. Wishing it were different is the expensive option.
Use the 5-step process: goals → problems → diagnosis → design → execution.
Ego and blind spots are the two barriers. Both feel like conviction from inside.
Be radically open-minded. Fear of looking wrong is more costly than being wrong.
Thoughtful disagreement: stress-test with believable people rather than argue to win.
Believability-weighted decision making — not all opinions carry equal weight.
Distinguish the machine from yourself. Look at your organisation from above as a designer.
Problems are fuel. Do not tolerate them, but do not hide them either.
Diagnose root causes before designing. Most people jump straight to solutions.
People are wired very differently. Match the person to the role's actual requirements.
Write your principles down. Undocumented principles are moods.
Everything is a machine producing outcomes. Fix the machine, not the instance.
learnings: Reflection is the step that converts a bad experience into an asset.
Weight opinions by track record, not seniority or volume.
Diagnosis before design is the discipline almost everyone skips.
Writing principles down is what makes them testable.
examples: Dalio's 1982 debt-crisis call was catastrophically wrong, cost him the firm, and became the origin of his entire radical-transparency method.
Bridgewater records nearly every meeting so decisions can be audited by anyone. Discomfort is the design goal.
The Dot Collector rates people live in meetings, making believability visible instead of political.
adapt: Write the trading principles down. 'Regime filter, structure stop, 48h horizon' beats remembering.
The alert flood is a machine problem, not a bad day. Diagnose the lifecycle rule, don't just clear the backlog.
Believability weighting on market opinions: the backtest outranks anyone's conviction, including yours.
Pain + reflection: the Meta restriction is only useful if the caption scoring process changes because of it.

interview_tech.q: How do you account for customer loyalty points under IFRS 15?
interview_tech.a: Points are a separate performance obligation. You allocate part of the original transaction price to the points based on their standalone selling price, adjusted for expected breakage, and defer that portion as contract liability. Revenue is recognised when points are redeemed or expire. Practically: the deferral reduces reported revenue today, and the breakage estimate is a judgement auditors probe every year. Retailers who ignore this overstate current-period revenue and get a restatement.

interview_tech.q: A category has 40% gross margin but negative contribution. How?
interview_tech.a: Gross margin ignores everything below the line. That category may carry disproportionate space, handling cost, markdown, shrink or return rate. Bulky low-value goods are the classic case — good percentage margin, terrible margin per square metre per week. Move to a contribution view: gross profit less directly attributable space, labour, logistics and markdown. Assortment decisions made on gross margin percentage alone are how retailers end up with profitable-looking categories that lose money.

interview_soft.q: What would your last manager say is your weakness?
interview_soft.a: Name a real one with a boundary. The pattern that works: a genuine weakness, evidence you know its cost, and the specific mechanism you use to contain it. 'I go too deep into detail before surfacing a view — it has cost me time on low-stakes analysis. I now set a decision deadline before starting and present at that point regardless of how complete it feels.' Avoid perfectionism, avoid anything that would disqualify you for the role itself.

interview_soft.q: What is the hardest decision you have made in your career?
interview_soft.a: Hard means genuinely two-sided, not merely unpleasant. Redundancies, closing a site, overruling someone you respected, or choosing between two people for one role. Structure: the trade-off, the information you had and did not have, how you decided, what it cost, and what you would do differently. Interviewers discount any answer where the right choice was obvious in hindsight — say what made it genuinely close.

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: avoid moving the f‑pawn before castling; your king stayed exposed, costing ~30 centipawn accuracy.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your 67 % win rate masks a dangerous habit: you consistently over‑extend in the Sicilian Defense, where you lose the majority of your points. Stop trying to out‑attack opponents who are already ahead; instead, adopt a solid, prophylactic setup—e.g., the London System or a Classical Caro‑Kann—and focus on piece coordination rather than speculative attacks. From the next game onward, play only the first 10–12 moves of a proven, low‑risk opening, then reassess the position before committing to any tactical fireworks.
